clips.text_en_b1: Bitcoin vs Gold. If you had to hold only one for the next 10 years, would you choose Bitcoin or gold? What makes your choice better than the other? Gold has been the safe store of value for thousands of years, but BTC is digital and limited to 21 million coins. Some /biz/ anons swear by gold, others say BTC will eat its lunch.

signal.rationale: Forced-choice debate post, no directional setup, anons split

clips.text_en_b2: For a ten-year long-only position, would you rather hold Bitcoin or gold, and what actually justifies your pick? Gold has anchored value for millennia, whereas BTC remains digital and capped at twenty-one million coins. On /biz/, anons split sharply: gold bugs point to its proven track record, while BTC maximalists insist it will eventually eat gold's lunch entirely.
clips.text_en_c1: Forced into a ten-year long-only position, would you allocate capital to Bitcoin or gold, and on what grounds does your selection outperform the alternative? Gold has anchored portfolios as a store of value across millennia, whereas BTC, a purely digital asset capped at twenty-one million coins, embodies scarcity in algorithmic form. Adherents on /biz/ remain divided: bullion loyalists cite durability, while Bitcoin maximalists insist it will cannibalise gold's monetary premium entirely. Given that BTC's volatility is breathtaking in both directions, the risk-adjusted calculus hinges on one's conviction regarding digital sovereignty versus time-tested metallurgical trust. Neither is obviously superior, but the asymmetry of outcomes is precisely what makes the comparison irresistible.
clips.text_en_c2: Were one compelled to commit capital for the ensuing decade, the perennial contest between Bitcoin and gold resists any facile adjudication. Gold, with its millennia-long track record as a repository of value, embodies a conservatism that has weathered empires and devaluations alike; yet its appreciation, though steady, seldom thrills. Bitcoin, by contrast, is a digital artefact of predetermined scarcity, capped at twenty-one million units, whose volatility is matched only by its capacity for asymmetric upside. The schism on /biz/ is hardly novel: gold maximalists invoke civilisational precedent, while BTC partisans counter that digital scarcity will inexorably devour its analog rival.

This marks the third major lockup release since the IPO, and the additional supply hitting the market could weigh heavily on sentiment.
clips.text_en_c1: On the ninth of September 2026, approximately 319 million SpaceX shares, constituting roughly seven percent of the baseline pool and around 2.4 percent of total shares outstanding, will exit the post-IPO lockup window. This date marks the ninetieth trading day since the listing and constitutes the third tranche of restrictions releasing into the open market. Should secondary supply flood the float within a compressed timeframe, short-term price discovery could prove punishing even for a name as institutionally favoured as SpaceX. Lockup events have historically functioned as overhead resistance; whether fundamentals or mere mechanics dictate the next move remains the operative question for traders.
clips.text_en_c2: On the ninth of September 2026, SpaceX confronts its third major lockup expiry, a corporate milestone whose consequences extend well beyond routine technicality. Approximately 319 million shares, constituting roughly 7 percent of the baseline pool and 2.4 percent of total shares outstanding, become eligible for sale precisely on the ninetieth trading day following the IPO. That such tranche releases occur in staggered waves is by design, yet the cumulative supply pressure is substantial enough to merit scrutiny. Insiders who endured the statutory restriction now possess liquid optionality, and the market must price the probability of distribution against the prevailing appetite for risk. Whether this particular wave precipitates meaningful dilution or merely registers as a footnote depends on sentiment, secondary demand, and the broader appetite for exposure to private-equity-adjacent equities.

clips.text_zh: 成日叫人買ChatGPT/Claude paid tier，但Kimi、GLM、Qwen平到笑，性能已經90%。靠AI續命嘅廢柴覺得OK。👍
clips.text_en_b1: Why do you never see people telling others to spend a tiny fraction of the price on cheaper models like Kimi, GLM or Qwen, which give you easily 90% of the performance for maybe 10% of the cost? The paid tier of ChatGPT or Claude is great, but the gap is smaller than the shills pretend.
clips.source_hint: /g/ thread asking why no one recommends cheaper AI models
clips.text_en_b2: Why does nobody recommend cheaper alternatives like Kimi, GLM, or Qwen, which deliver roughly ninety percent of the performance at perhaps ten percent of what ChatGPT or Claude charge? The paid tiers are excellent, admittedly, but the actual gap is far narrower than the shills make out. Paying full price is essentially throwing money away.
clips.text_en_c1: It is striking how rarely anyone recommends the affordable alternatives to ChatGPT or Claude's premium tier, given that models such as Kimi, GLM, and Qwen routinely deliver approximately ninety percent of frontier performance at perhaps a tenth of the subscription cost. The marketing apparatus surrounding proprietary incumbents has evidently convinced a generation of knowledge workers that excellence is inseparable from a monthly invoice. Whether this perception reflects genuine capability gaps or merely the gravitational pull of brand prestige is debatable. For routine drafting, summarisation, and boilerplate reasoning, the cheaper models are, frankly, indistinguishable to all but the most demanding evaluators, rendering the markup indefensible.
clips.text_en_c2: It is a peculiarity of contemporary discourse that evangelism for ChatGPT or Claude's premium tiers proceeds unchallenged, while ostensibly equivalent alternatives languish in obscurity. Chinese-origin models such as Kimi, GLM, and Qwen now deliver what is, by any reasonable benchmark, ninety percent of frontier performance at perhaps a tenth of the subscription cost, yet one rarely encounters their proponents proselytising with comparable fervour. The disparity is instructive: shilling is, after all, a function of incentives, and the affiliate economics of premium Western tiers evidently outweigh the modest commissions available from domestic competitors. For users whose requirements remain prosaic, the rational calculus increasingly favours the cheaper alternative, notwithstanding the prestige conferred by a recognisable subscription. The gap narrows with each release cycle.

clips.text_en_b1: 21 U.S. banks plan to launch a joint stablecoin. The real purpose behind Trump's stablecoin bill is to let private companies and banks issue their own currencies. Soon you'll see Apple Coin, Google Coin, Microsoft Coin, Tesla Coin, X Coin, Bank Coin. The U.S. markets will be flooded with hundreds of digital cash tokens.

signal.rationale: Macro news observation, no actionable setup

clips.text_en_b2: Twenty-one U.S. banks are jointly launching a stablecoin, and the underlying purpose of Trump's bill is to let private firms and financial institutions mint their own currencies. Once that door opens, we will likely see Apple Coin, Google Coin, Microsoft Coin, Tesla Coin, and X Coin flooding the market with countless digital tokens.
clips.text_en_c1: Twenty-one American banks are reportedly coalescing around a jointly issued stablecoin, ostensibly under legislation championed by the Trump administration whose underlying purpose appears to be licensing private issuers to mint their own digital cash. If this framework advances, the near-term landscape will likely feature branded tokens from Apple, Google, Microsoft, Tesla, and X, alongside bespoke instruments from individual financial institutions. Hundreds of such instruments could plausibly circulate, fragmenting liquidity rather than consolidating it. Whether Hong Kong's tightly regulated dollar-peg ecosystem can retain relevance amid this onslaught of corporatised monetary tokens is doubtful; the regime risks being diluted into irrelevance by sheer proliferation.
clips.text_en_c2: Twenty-one American banking institutions have coalesced around a joint stablecoin initiative, ostensibly a stride toward payment modernisation, though the underlying legislative architecture suggests something rather more ambitious. The Trump administration's stablecoin framework, whatever its public rationalisation, effectively grants private enterprise and chartered banks the prerogative to mint their own digital tender. The implications, if one extends the logic to its terminus, are staggering: an imminent proliferation of branded tokens, Apple Coin, Google Coin, Microsoft Coin, Tesla Coin, X Coin, ad infinitum, each a sovereign-adjacent liability masquerading as innovation. Hong Kong, whose monetary discipline has long served as regional ballast, will find itself diluted by transborder liquidity flows it cannot regulate. The American bazaar, it appears, has discovered tokenisation.

clips.text_en_b1: Character dynamics like this are illegal in western video games. Screenshots from the post show multiple named NPCs reacting to each other across scenes.
clips.source_hint: /v/ thread praising Eastern game character dynamics

signal.rationale: Gaming culture post, not a trade

clips.text_en_b2: Character dynamics executed at this level should frankly be illegal in Western RPGs. The /v/ thread highlights how Eastern titles weave layered relationships between party members across countless scenes, while Western developers largely keep their NPC interactions flat and uninspired. The attached screenshots showcase named characters reacting dynamically to one another.
clips.text_en_c1: Character dynamics of this calibre remain conspicuously absent from western RPG design, a deficit that /v/ has been cataloguing with considerable frustration. Eastern titles invest in layered, asymmetric relationships between party members, allowing named NPCs to register as discrete personalities whose interactions evolve across scenes and arcs. Western studios, by contrast, tend to treat companion characters as interchangeable quest dispensers, stripped of interior life. The screenshots circulating demonstrate precisely this contrast: portraits reacting, conflicting, and accruing history. Until western writers internalise that meaningful characterisation requires friction rather than exposition dumps, the gap will only widen.
clips.text_en_c2: Character dynamics of this calibre remain, as the /v/ consensus rightly observes, essentially proscribed within the western RPG tradition. Eastern developers, working from a fundamentally different narrative inheritance, cultivate interpersonal relationships whose evolution unfolds across dozens of granular beats, with party members whose grievances, affections, and betrayals accrue cumulative weight over the course of a hundred-hour campaign. Western titles, by contrast, persist in reducing companion characterisation to binary approval metrics, a mechanical flattening that strips relationships of their inherent ambiguity. The screenshots circulated in the original thread depict named NPCs whose reactions to one another register genuine texture across scenes. Whether this disparity reflects cultural disposition, design inertia, or simply divergent assumptions about player patience is debatable, but the qualitative gulf is undeniable.

clips.text_en_c1: A new deadlift world record has been ratified, and the Nordic strongman contingent is processing what can only be described as a collective blow. Thor's previously dominant mark fell to a Mexican competitor whose pull, executed under full competition conditions, is documented on YouTube for sceptical posterity. The standard for elite strongman pulling continues its inexorable upward drift, with each generation rewriting the ceiling that seemed immutable a decade prior. Whether Thor mounts a response in his next sanctioned appearance will determine whether this represents a transitional moment or the genuine changing of the guard.
clips.text_en_c2: The barbell has once again been pulled into uncharted territory, and the Nordic strongman fraternity finds itself in a state of collective unease. A formidable Mexican competitor has eclipsed Thor's deadlift record, the lift executed under proper contest conditions and now circulating across strength-sport media with the customary velocity. That elite strongman pulling standards continue their inexorable ascent should surprise no one, as the sport's competitive depth has expanded considerably over the past decade, with athletes from previously peripheral federations now training under optimal protocols. For the recreational lifter nursing a recalcitrant lower back after deadlift work, the spectacle serves as both inspiration and humbling reminder: the parameters of human capability are revised with each meet, and the ceiling, it seems, refuses to settle.

clips.text_en_c1: Reading Chainsaw Man volumes six and seven, the Reze arc initially encountered via cinema rather than its original print iteration, has proven genuinely compelling when experienced through Tatsuki Fujimoto's panel compositions. Critics were quick to deride season one's direction as visually inert, yet the cinematic framing aligns remarkably well with material that was always conceived in cinematic terms. Whether subsequent adaptations can replicate the manga's idiosyncratic pacing remains doubtful, since static page-turning rewards an interiority that animated brevity tends to compress. For now, the printed source remains unambiguously superior to its televised counterpart.
clips.text_en_c2: Chainsaw Man's sixth and seventh volumes reward the reader who arrives at them via the Reze arc's cinematic adaptation, the recent film having imparted a visual vocabulary that enriches rather than competes with Tatsuki Fujimoto's source material. The panel compositions possess a distinctly kinetic sensibility, each splash page calibrated with the precision one might associate with storyboard art rather than conventional manga convention. Critics of the anime's first season derided its direction as idiosyncratic; yet, upon returning to the printed page, one appreciates how faithfully Fujimoto's framing anticipated that very aesthetic, a confluence of static and motion that suits the narrative's propulsive rhythms. For the reader grinding through professional examinations and seeking decompression, the series offers precisely the kind of calculated mayhem that restores equilibrium.
